content.title: About
content.content: Buckwheat is a groat made from the seeds of the common buckwheat plant (Fagopyrum esculentum). Despite its name, it is not a grain and is not related to wheat: it belongs to the knotweed family, like sorrel and rhubarb. Buckwheat has a nutty, slightly earthy flavor. It is cooked as porridge or a side dish, added to soups and salads, and its flour is used for pancakes and noodles.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Buckwheat is a pseudocereal: its seeds are used like a grain, but the plant is not a cereal.
Buckwheat is naturally gluten-free, but it may be contaminated with gluten during processing.
Roasted buckwheat is dark and aromatic, while green (unroasted) buckwheat is paler and milder.
Buckwheat flour is used to make pancakes, galettes, and Japanese soba noodles.
Bees make dark, aromatic honey from buckwheat nectar.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: Buckwheat contains protein with a good amino acid profile, including lysine, which is low in many grains.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion and helps you feel full.

items.title: Contains magnesium, copper, and manganese
items.content: These minerals support muscle and nerve function and metabolism.

items.title: Contains rutin
items.content: Rutin is a flavonoid with antioxidant properties.

items.title: Suitable for gluten-free diets
items.content: Pure buckwheat without cross-contamination can be part of a gluten-free diet when properly labeled.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Buckwheat allergy can be severe and is sometimes linked with latex allergy.

items.title: Gluten contamination
items.content: People with celiac disease should choose buckwheat labeled gluten-free because of possible cross-contamination.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: A sudden increase in fiber intake can cause bloating and discomfort.

items.title: Carbohydrates
items.content: Buckwheat contains carbohydrates, so people with diabetes should keep an eye on portion size.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Rinse buckwheat, add water in a ratio of about 1 to 2, bring to a boil, reduce the heat, and cook covered for 15–20 minutes, then let it stand. Serve it as a side dish or add it to soups, salads, fillings, and patties. Green buckwheat can be soaked and sprouted.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry groats in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Buckwheat flour spoils faster, so keep it in the refrigerator. Store cooked buckwheat in the refrigerator for 3–4 days.

hot-chocolate-cocoa-dry-mix-made-with-lo.title: Hot chocolate / cocoa, dry mix, made with low‑fat (1 %) or fat‑free (skim) milk

content.title: About
content.content: The dry mix for hot chocolate/cocoa is designed to be prepared with low‑fat (1 %) or completely fat‑free (skim) milk. The blend contains cocoa powder, sugar and emulsifiers, delivering a rich chocolate flavor without added fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The mix dissolves quickly in hot milk, creating a smooth, lump‑free beverage.
Cocoa powder is usually gently processed to retain most of its antioxidants.
Low‑fat milk provides most of the calcium and protein while keeping saturated fat to a minimum.
The product is widely used in cafés and cafeterias for fast preparation of hot drinks.
Some versions include vanilla or a pinch of sea salt to enhance flavor.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Cocoa is high in flavonoids, which help combat free radicals and support cardiovascular health.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Preparing the drink with low‑fat milk keeps saturated fat intake low, which is beneficial for weight management.

items.title: Source of magnesium and potassium
items.content: Both the cocoa mix and milk supply magnesium and potassium, essential for muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Mood‑boosting compounds
items.content: Cocoa contains phenylethylamine, which may improve mood and increase alertness.

items.title: Provides protein
items.content: Skim milk adds high‑quality protein to the beverage, supporting tissue repair and satiety.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or a cow‑milk protein allergy should choose a dairy‑free alternative.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: The mix often contains added sugar; individuals monitoring blood glucose should watch portion size.

items.title: Caffeine and theobromine
items.content: Cocoa contains modest amounts of theobromine, which can affect sleep if consumed in large quantities.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Cocoa contains oxalates that may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible individuals.

content.title: How to Prepare
content.content: Combine 2–3 tablespoons of the dry mix with 250 ml of hot (but not boiling) low‑fat or skim milk. Stir vigorously with a whisk or blend until fully dissolved. Optionally add a pinch of salt or a dash of vanilla extract.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dry mix in a sealed container in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Check the package for the best‑by date; after opening, use within 3–6 months for optimal quality.

content.title: About
content.content: Soy milk is a plant‑based beverage made from soybeans that are ground, cooked, and filtered. The sweetened version contains added sugar or other sweeteners, giving it a pleasant, mild sweetness. It is a popular alternative to cow’s milk for people with lactose intolerance, vegans, and those seeking a lower‑calorie drink.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Commercial soy milk production began in the United States in the 1930s.
Soy milk provides roughly the same amount of protein as cow’s milk (about 3 g per 100 ml).
Sweetened varieties are often fortified with calcium, vitamin D, and vitamin B12.
Soybeans are a source of isoflavones, which are studied for potential heart‑health and hormonal benefits.
In Japan, soy milk is commonly served chilled during the summer months.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Soy protein contains all essential amino acids, making it a valuable protein source for vegetarians and vegans.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Unlike whole cow’s milk, soy milk is primarily composed of polyunsaturated fats, which are heart‑friendly.

items.title: Source of isoflavones
items.content: Isoflavones may support hormonal balance and contribute to reduced risk of osteoporosis.

items.title: Fortified with calcium and vitamins
items.content: Most commercial versions are enriched with calcium, vitamin D, and vitamin B12, helping to replace nutrients typically obtained from dairy.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Sweetened soy milk often contains added probiotics that promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to soy proteins, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Added sugar content
items.content: Sweetened versions can contain significant amounts of added sugar, which is undesirable for people with diabetes or those monitoring weight.

items.title: Phytates
items.content: Soy contains phytates that can reduce the absorption of certain minerals (iron, zinc) when consumed in excess.

items.title: Genetically modified organisms (GMOs)
items.content: The majority of soybeans grown worldwide are GMO; those avoiding GMOs should look for certified organic options.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sweetened soy milk can be enjoyed straight, added to smoothies, oatmeal, baked goods, coffee, or used as a base for sauces. For extra flavor, consider adding cinnamon, vanilla, or a dash of cocoa.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store an opened carton in the refrigerator and consume within 5‑7 days. Keep unopened packages in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Discard if the milk develops a sour smell or off‑taste.
